work_order.confidence_rationale: I did not take either the QA report or the previous plan on trust. I unpacked the failing run's trace, read the page snapshot and the screenshot behind T-2, and then drove the real makeAsNonChildTransactions through a probe on the PR head: the never-filled, the under-filled, the single-child and the opposite-sign shapes all return a survivor with payee: null, and the split-out shape returns rows with the payee intact. That set is exactly the set QA failed and the set QA passed, which is what makes this a cause and not a correlation. I then applied the one-line fix and ran the full loot-core node suite from the repository root: 87 files passed, 1297 tests passed, 1 expected failure, and nothing regressed. Held below 90 for two reasons: I verified the survivor's field set against the two code paths that build one, not against every producer of a split parent in the app, and the corrected AC-3 and AC-5 examples are corrections to how QA should drive the register, which I reasoned from the error-context snapshot and the helper's own header comment rather than by driving a browser myself in this session.
work_order.understanding:
THE PREVIOUS PLAN WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE AMOUNTS AND WRONG ABOUT WHICH FUNCTION WAS DEFECTIVE, AND IT SHIPPED NO TEST THAT COULD HAVE SEEN THE DEFECT.

What the previous plan got right: its arithmetic rewrite is correct and is now on the branch. The two-sided `promotedRowsAccountForParent` relation, the magnitude comparison, the parent-less-what-left subtraction on the keep branch, the `error: null` on the single-child return, and the three-distinct-categories test are all sound, all shipped, and all still pass on the PR head. I did not disturb any of it.

What it got wrong: it enumerated the fields the surviving row needs and got `error` and `amount` right, but it never checked `payee` — the one field `splitTransaction` deliberately moves OFF the parent and onto the children. So it built a survivor that is arithmetically perfect and semantically a different transaction from the one the user split. The plan's diagnosis pointed at `makeAsNonChildTransactions`'s guard, where the amounts are written; the defect is one level down in the helper that builds the row, `makeTransactionWithChildCategory`, which is called on both keep-parent paths and takes `category` from the promoted row but leaves `payee` inherited from the parent.

That is why the whole unit suite is green while 10 of 15 browser checks fail. Every one of the 19 cases in the `unsplitting a split` block asserts through the `asRows` helper, which destructures `{ id, amount }` and nothing else, or asserts `error` / `category` / `schedule`. Not one asserts `payee`. The suite is not weakly passing; it is blind to this axis by construction, and the previous plan's own test list kept it that way.

What QA actually saw. The five tests that pass are the ones whose rows come back with the payee attached: T-5, T-6, T-9 and T-14 take the split-OUT branch, which returns the promoted children, and `makeChild` copies the parent's payee onto them, so those rows render normally. The ten that fail are the ones that go through `makeTransactionWithChildCategory`: T-1, T-2, T-3, T-8, T-12 and T-15 report `Array []` — no rows matching the payee at all — and T-4 and T-13 report one EXTRA row. Not one of the ten reports a wrong amount. `error-context.md` for T-2 settles it: the search box holds "QA Fixture A" and the register body reads "No transactions", and the screenshot confirms it. The row was never lost. It is invisible to a payee-filtered view because it has no payee.

Date of the bug. I probed the pre-PR code too. On main, the all-zero arm already returned a payee-less survivor, so this defect predates PR #100. What PR #100 did was widen the keep-parent branch from "all promoted rows are zero" to "promoted rows do not account for the parent", which drags every under-fill shape — 5000/0, opposite-sign pairs, partially typed legs — onto the path that loses the payee. So the previous plan did not create the bug; it multiplied its reach and shipped no test that could see it.

TWO OF QA'S TEN FAILURES ARE NOT PRODUCT DEFECTS, AND I AM NOT CHASING THEM AS IF THEY WERE.

(a) T-7 and T-11 never reach the product. Both die inside QA's own `addSplit` helper at `waiting for getByTestId('add-button')`. The helper's own header comment states why: the editing row replaces its Add button with an "Amount left: …" strip whenever the split has an outstanding difference, so an under-filled or over-filled split cannot be committed from the new-transaction row at all. Both fixtures ask for legs that do not sum to the parent. The product is never exercised, so there is nothing in the register to fix. The reachable route is to commit a correctly filled split and then edit one leg upward — which is also the only route AC-5's worked example should name, so I corrected that example (below) rather than leaving a criterion QA cannot execute.

(b) T-4 and T-13 report a row count that is off by one, in QA's favour of being too small. The fixture builds FOUR legs, unsplits one, and expects four rows total. One promoted leg plus three legs still standing behind the kept parent is four rows at 0.00, plus the parent at 123.45 — five. AC-3's own rule already says the unsplit leg "stands alone at 0.00", which is a row, not an absence. The product's arithmetic here is right and money-conserving, and I verified it by probe.

Both (a) and (b) are criterion-example problems, and root-cause.md puts correcting a criterion in my hands. In each case the RULE the criterion states is correct and the code agrees with it; what is wrong is the worked example, which describes a route the register will not perform (a) or miscounts the rows the rule produces (b). I am correcting the examples and saying exactly that. I am not touching AC-1, AC-2, AC-4, AC-6 through AC-12, and I am not touching the rule AC-3 or AC-5 state. If the code were the thing that were wrong, this work order would say so instead.
work_order.root_cause: `makeTransactionWithChildCategory` builds the surviving row by spreading the split parent and overriding only `is_parent` and `category`. But `splitTransaction` sets `payee: null` on the parent when the split is opened, because it moves the payee down onto the children; `makeChild` is what puts it there. So every survivor this helper produces inherits `payee: null` from a parent that by construction no longer carries one, and `makeTransactionWithChildCategory` never takes it back. The row survives in the database with the correct amount and category and no payee at all, which is why every unit test passes and every browser check fails: the row is not gone, it is invisible to any payee-filtered view of the register. The defect is pre-existing on the all-zero arm; PR #100 widened the arm from "promoted rows are all zero" to "promoted rows do not account for the parent", dragging every under-fill shape onto the payee-losing path.
work_order.approach:
Take the payee from the row the category is already taken from.

`makeTransactionWithChildCategory(parent, data)` is the single helper that builds the surviving row on both keep-parent paths — the single-child early return at transactions.ts:457 and the guarded branch at :515 — and it already reads one field off the promoted row (`category: data.category || null`). The fix is one line beside it: `payee: data.payee ?? parent.payee`. The promoted row is where the payee still lives, it is the row the register actually shows, and taking both fields from the same row gives them one provenance instead of two. The `??` parent fallback is the degenerate case, where the caller passed the parent itself because nothing was promoted; it cannot make anything worse, since that parent's payee is null too.

This is deliberately NOT the same approach as the previous plan's, and the difference is the whole point: the previous plan rewrote which rows an amount comparison runs over, in `makeAsNonChildTransactions`. That rewrite is correct and it stays. This work order changes one field on one helper and touches no arithmetic at all, because the arithmetic is not what is broken.

The trap to avoid is over-correction. The obvious wrong fix is to force the parent's payee onto every row this function returns, or to change `splitTransaction` so the parent keeps its payee. Both would corrupt the split-OUT branch, which correctly returns each child with its OWN payee — a child whose payee the user retyped must not be stamped with the parent's. The fix is scoped to the survivor, and the tests pin both directions so the next attempt cannot widen it.

On the tests: the reason this shipped green the first time is that `asRows` destructures `{ id, amount }`, so the `unsplitting a split` block is structurally incapable of seeing a payee. The new cases assert `payee` directly on the returned rows rather than through `asRows`, on each shape QA reported — never-filled, under-filled, single-child, opposite-sign — and a case asserts the split-OUT branch still returns each child's own payee, so the fix cannot be widened into a regression. I confirmed the fix by applying it and running the full loot-core node suite: 1297 passed, 1 expected failure, 0 failed.

files.change: In `makeTransactionWithChildCategory` (the helper at :110-119 that builds the surviving row on both keep-parent paths), add `payee: data.payee ?? parent.payee` beside the existing `category: data.category || null`, with a short comment naming why the parent's payee cannot be inherited: `splitTransaction` sets `payee: null` on a parent when the split opens and moves the payee onto the children, so a survivor built from the parent alone comes back payee-less and drops out of any payee-filtered view. Take it from the same promoted row the category comes from so both fields share one provenance. Change nothing else in this file — the amount arithmetic, the `promotedRowsAccountForParent` relation, the magnitude comparison and the `error: null` clearances from the previous plan all stay exactly as they are on the branch.
files.why: This is the only place a surviving row is constructed. Every one of QA's ten failures runs through it; every one of QA's five passes does not. The field is wrong there and nowhere else.

files.change: Add cases to the existing `describe('unsplitting a split')` block that assert `payee` on the returned rows directly rather than through the `asRows` helper, which destructures only `{ id, amount }` and is why 19 green cases missed this: one per shape QA reported (never-filled, one leg typed and one empty, the single-child early return, and opposite-sign legs that fall short), each with the parent carrying `payee: 'payee-parent'` and the split already opened so the parent is `payee: null`; each asserting the survivor carries `payee-parent`. Add a case asserting the split-OUT branch is unchanged: a correctly filled split whose children carry a payee different from the parent's returns rows carrying the CHILDREN's payee, so a fix that stamps the parent's payee everywhere goes red. Name the cases for the provenance they pin, in the style of the existing ones.

qa_script: The PR title must begin with `[AI] ` — `.github/agents/pr-and-commit-rules.md` makes that mandatory for every agent-authored PR, and PR #81 shipped without it and it was filed as a finding against that PR. Apply it yourself; the pipeline does not.

Search the register by payee before asserting anything about a surviving row. Six of the ten failures read as `Array []` purely because the survivor had no payee to match; an unfiltered row count would not have noticed. This is the habit that separates 'the row is wrong' from 'the row is invisible', and it is what AC-13 turns into a criterion.

Build a never-filled or under-filled split by committing a correctly filled one and blanking legs on the saved row. The register will not commit a split whose legs do not sum to the parent: the editing row swaps its Add button for an 'Amount left: …' strip, and waiting on the Add button is a 20s timeout that never reaches the product. This is what T-7 and T-11 hit.
Build an over-filled split the same way — commit 50.00 / 73.45 on a 123.45 parent, then raise one leg to 70.00. AC-5's arm is only reachable that way.

A three-or-more-leg split is built as FOUR legs; the split editor opens with two and 'Add Split' adds two at a time. After unsplitting ONE leg of a four-leg split, expect FIVE rows for that payee, not four: the parent, the promoted leg, and the three legs still behind it. T-4 and T-13 asserted four.

Do not read a wrong amount as a wrong amount without checking the payee first. Not one of the ten failures reported a wrong figure; they reported a missing row. The arithmetic in this function is correct on the branch and this change does not touch it.

Confirm `yarn workspace @actual-app/core run test` and `yarn typecheck` both pass from the repository root, and that the nineteen pre-existing `unsplitting a split` cases are still green — they assert only `{ id, amount }`, so if they moved, something changed that this fix was not supposed to change.
risks: The fix reads a field off `data` on a parameter typed `Partial<TransactionEntity>`, and `data` is a promoted child in the normal case but can be the parent itself when nothing was promoted (the `?? parentTransaction` fallback at :521). The `??` keeps that degenerate case from getting worse — the parent's payee is null there too — but it means the payee's provenance is 'the row the category came from', not 'a child'. The comment must say so, or the next reader will assume a stronger guarantee than exists.

`payee` is not the only field `splitTransaction` moves or clears on the parent. This change covers the one QA demonstrated. `subtransactions` and `is_parent` are handled by the two callers in Account.tsx, and I verified those paths through the reducer but did not drive the app, so a sibling field with the same shape of defect would not have shown up here.

The fix could be over-applied by someone reading the symptom rather than the helper: stamping the parent's payee on every row, or changing `splitTransaction` to stop nulling the parent, both break the split-out path. AC-15 and the split-out case in tests[] exist to catch that; they only help if the implementer runs them.

Two of QA's ten failures (T-7, T-11) were never product failures — they timed out in QA's own fixture helper. If the corrected AC-5 example is not followed, those will fail again for the same reason and this work order will look wrong. That is a real risk and the reason AC-5's worked example was corrected rather than left alone.

AC-3's corrected example now states a five-row expectation. If the implementer reads that as licence to change the row count in the code, they will break the rule the criterion states. The count is in the example, not the rule, and the rule is what the code already satisfies.
out_of_scope: Why the pre-existing all-zero arm lost the payee before this PR. It is dated and described here, and the single-line fix covers it, but no change is proposed to how or when that arm was introduced.

The parent in the keep-parent branch inherits its SplitTransactionError rather than having it recomputed, so a parent whose amount changes can carry a stale split badge. Pre-existing, unchanged by this work, and fixing it means touching error handling. The previous plan already recorded it here.

Whether the parent or the first selected child should win the surviving row's category. Child-wins is pinned as deliberate by the existing single-child test and the previous plan left it; making the parent win is a behaviour change needing a maintainer's call, and this change deliberately does not disturb it.

QA's fixture helpers (`qa-evidence/.../spec/helpers.ts`) are QA's, not the product's. The two routes they cannot perform are corrected here as criterion examples rather than by asking anyone to change the suite.

Probe against the REAL `makeAsNonChildTransactions` on the PR head (parent payee moved onto children, i.e. parent `payee: null`): never-filled, under-filled, single-child and opposite-sign shapes each return `updated: [{ id: 'p', amount: 12345, payee: null, is_parent: false }]`; the split-out shape returns the promoted children with `payee: 'PAYEE_X'` intact. Code: `splitTransaction` (transactions.ts:386-415) returns `{ ...rest, is_parent: true, payee: null, … }`. `makeChild` (:57-83) sets `payee: 'payee' in data ? data.payee : parent.payee`. `makeTransactionWithChildCategory` (:110-119) spreads the parent and overrides only `is_parent` and `category`. It is called at :460 and :519 — the only two constructions of a surviving row.

Rendering: `useDisplayPayee` reads `transaction.payee` for a row with no subtransactions, and null renders as an empty string. That is the mechanism by which a surviving row matches no `hasText: payee` filter.

Why 19 unit cases stayed green: `asRows` at transactions.test.ts:457 destructures `{ id, amount }` only. Every assertion in the block goes through it, or checks `error` / `category` / `schedule`. None reads `payee`.

T-7/T-11 are not product failures: `qa-evidence/.../spec/helpers.ts` header, lines 18-21 — 'The editing row replaces its Add button with an "Amount left: … / Distribute / Add Split" error strip whenever the split has an outstanding difference, so an under-filled split cannot be committed from that row.' Both fixtures pass legs that do not sum to the parent, so `addSplit` times out at :276 and the product is never exercised.

T-4/T-13 row arithmetic: the fixture builds four legs (`['50.00','40.00','30.00','3.45']`), unsplits one, and expects four rows. One promoted leg plus three still behind the kept parent is four rows at 0.00, plus the parent at 123.45 — five. AC-3's own rule already says the unsplit leg stands alone at 0.00, which is a row.

alternatives_considered.approach: Patch `makeAsNonChildTransactions` to restore the payee on the rows it returns — set `payee: parentTransaction.payee ?? <promoted child's payee>` at each of the two keep-parent return sites.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Same one line of effect, worse place. The helper is what makes the row, so the invariant 'a survivor carries the payee of the row it was promoted from' would live in three call sites instead of one, and the two branches could drift. It also leaves the single-child early return and the guarded branch free to disagree about the field, which is the exact inconsistency AC-8 was written to end.

alternatives_considered.approach: Change `splitTransaction` to stop nulling the parent's payee, so the survivor inherits it correctly and nothing downstream changes.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Corrects the symptom by breaking the model. The parent is `payee: null` on purpose because the payee belongs to the legs once a split exists; the register renders a split parent from its children. Re-populating it would put a second, divergent copy of the payee on the parent, and every consumer that reads a parent's payee would now see a value that only some children agree with.

alternatives_considered.approach: Force the parent's payee onto every row `makeTransactionWithChildCategory` returns, on the reasoning that the survivor inherits the parent's whole identity.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Breaks the split-OUT branch, which is the one that already works. `makeChild` gives each child the parent's payee only as a default; a leg the user retyped carries its own, and a correct split-out must return that leg's payee. QA's T-5, T-6, T-9 and T-14 pass today and would go red. Rejected as the over-correction AC-15 exists to prevent.

alternatives_considered.approach: Change `useDisplayPayee` to fall back to a split parent's first child's payee when the row's own payee is null.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Treats the symptom where it is rendered and leaves the database row wrong. Every other consumer of that transaction — sync, the API, the rules engine, exports — would still see `payee: null`, and the row would remain invisible to anything that filters on the field rather than rendering it. The defect is that the row was built wrong, not that it was displayed wrong.

alternatives_considered.approach: Treat this as two identical failures and write stop.json — the previous plan's approach has now failed twice.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This is not the same approach failing twice. PR #100 implemented the previous plan's arithmetic rewrite and QA's five arithmetic checks pass (T-5, T-6, T-9, T-10, T-14); the ten failures are a different field on a different function, which the previous plan never looked at. A `failure-packet.json` is also absent, so this is a QA verdict rather than a mechanically unbuildable plan. The new approach changes the file and the function the old one targeted, so a third attempt along these lines is not what is being proposed.

alternatives_considered.approach: Leave the two non-product failure classes alone and let the implementer discover them.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: QA is given no memory of what it found last time. T-7, T-11, T-4 and T-13 will fail identically on every future run until the criterion examples that produce them are corrected, and each of those failures reads like a product defect. Correcting the examples is the only durable fix and it is explicitly mine to make.

assumptions: `makeAsNonChildTransactions` is the only reducer that promotes a split parent into a surviving non-child row. I verified the two call sites in Account.tsx (~:1242 parent-selected and ~:1266 some-children-selected), both passing `options({ splits: 'grouped' })` and `ungroupTransaction`, and both reaching this function.

The payee a split's children carry is the payee the user originally typed, because `makeChild` copies it from the parent at the moment the split opens and `splitTransaction` pushes it down. A leg whose payee the user later retypes carries its own, which is why AC-15 pins the split-out direction rather than assuming a single payee.

QA's `fixtureRows` filter (`table.getByTestId('row').filter({ hasText: payee })`) is a legitimate model of what a user sees when they search the register, so a payee-less row's invisibility there is a real user-visible defect and not an artefact of the harness. The T-2 page snapshot and screenshot support this directly.

`asRows` in transactions.test.ts is the right helper for `[id, amount]` assertions and should stay; the new cases read `payee` off the returned rows directly rather than widening it, because widening it would touch all 19 existing assertions for no gain.
unknowns: Whether any other consumer of a split parent's payee reads it expecting null now that survivors carry one — sync, the API's transaction shapes, the rules engine, CSV/OFX export. I traced the register's render path and the two UI call sites; I did not audit every reader of the field.

Whether a parent that survives an unsplit with children still behind it (`deleteParentTransaction === false`) displays correctly in the register under a payee search. T-4 and T-13 exercised exactly that shape and returned all five rows through a payee filter, so it appears to, but the count was wrong for an unrelated reason and I did not re-verify that shape in isolation.

Whether the surviving row should carry the payee of the FIRST promoted child or of the parent as originally typed, on the two-child path where two legs with different payees are unsplit together. The fix takes the first promoted row's payee, matching what `category` already does and what the existing single-child test pins for category; if the parent's original payee is the right answer, that is the same maintainer's call the category finding was left at.
residual_risks: This fixes the field QA demonstrated. If a surviving row is wrong in some other way that QA's assertions did not compare — a wrong account, date, cleared flag or sort order — QA will keep finding it one run at a time, because the checks that failed here compared amounts and payees and nothing else.

T-7 and T-11 are corrected in the criteria, not in QA's suite. If the next QA run's helper is unchanged and the criterion examples are not followed literally, those two will fail again at the same 20s timeout on the Add button, having verified nothing.

AC-3's corrected example states a five-row expectation where the old one implied four. If QA's assertion is written from the old example rather than the corrected one, T-4 and T-13 will fail again for the same arithmetic reason, on a correct implementation.

The unit block is now payee-aware only in the new cases. A future change to `asRows`, or a rewrite of the block that consolidates the new assertions back through it, would silently restore the blindness that let this ship.

triage.diagnosis:
Not a flaky check and not an outage: PR #100's release note is malformed. The new file upcoming-release-notes/fix-unsplit-preserves-parent-amount.md contains no YAML front matter at all — it opens straight into the prose sentence 'Unsplitting a split no longer destroys...' — so gray-matter returns empty data and packages/ci-actions/bin/release-notes-gate.mjs reports all three rules it breaks at once (missing a category, missing authors, body should contain exactly one line, at validateNote(), gate lines 62-105). The body is a three-paragraph essay, which independently breaks the one-line rule. I reproduced it exactly: extracted the file from the PR head and ran validateNote() against it, getting the same three strings verbatim. Every other check was green — lage typecheck 10/10, lage test 8 of 9 tasks succeeding (@actual-app/core 1288 tests, web, sync-server, api, components, cli, crdt, eslint-plugin-actual), verify.build and verify.e2e both correctly skipped as unconfigured. The only red task was '@actual-app/ci-actions release-notes'. This is a real defect in the project's own code, inside what the work order already covers (PR #100's own release note), so the fix is a repair: prepend `---
category: Bugfixes
authors: [Shivam-Fl]
---` and collapse the body to the one sentence the contributor docs ask for. I confirmed the corrected shape passes — a front-matter-plus-one-line version returns [] from validateNote(). review.title: The single-child early return at transactions.ts:452-472 is the one branch the ticket's new relation never reaches, and this PR touches it (adding `error: null`) instead of deleting it. I built the counterfactual: remove the whole 21-line branch and the entire loot-core suite is still green — 1297 passed / 1 expected fail / 2 skipped, identical to the shipped run, including all 38 tests in transactions.test.ts. The branch is not merely redundant, it is wrong: on the shapes where it and the general path disagree, the general path is right. Parent 12345 with a single child of 20000, child unsplit -> branch returns `updated [p:12345] deleted [c0:20000]` (the user's typed 200.00 destroyed, row reads 123.45); without the branch the same input returns `updated [c0:20000] deleted [p:12345]`, exactly AC-5's overshoot arm. Across ten one-child shapes the branch matches the general path on six and is wrong on four — child equal, child over, zero parent with a non-zero child, negative parent with an overshooting child. Every disagreement destroys money.

`packages/loot-core/src/shared/transactions.ts:452`

Evidence: Counterfactual: deleted lines 452-472, re-ran `yarn workspace @actual-app/core run test` -> 87 passed | 1 skipped (88 files), 1297 passed | 1 expected fail | 2 skipped, byte-identical counts to the shipped suite. Ten-shape sweep against the real function, branch vs branch-removed: `child equal | preErr=null -> upd ["p|12345|false|"] del ["c0|12345|false|"]` (branch) vs `upd ["c0|12345|false|"] del ["p|12345|true|"]` (general path); `child over` (parent 12345, child 20000): branch `upd ["p|12345"] del ["c0:20000"]`, general path `upd ["c0:20000"] del ["p:12345"]`; `parent zero child nonzero`: branch keeps p at 0 and deletes a typed 5000, general path promotes the 5000. The branch is reachable and the general path already handles it: `TransactionsTable.tsx:3682` and `useTransactionBatchActions.ts:365` both call `deleteTransaction` on a single selected child, and `deleteTransaction` (`transactions.ts:366-372`) strips `is_parent` when one child remains. I drove that end to end: split 123.45 into 5000/7345, delete the 7345 leg, unsplit the survivor -> `updated [p:12345] deleted [c0:5000]`. The asymmetry is what makes the branch indefensible: it hardcodes `deleted: [childTransactionsToUpdate[0]]` and returns the PARENT as survivor, where the general path's rule is about which rows account for the parent. `origin/main` has the identical branch (verified by running the probe against main's copy of the file), so this is not preserved shipped behaviour — it is pre-existing and this PR is the right place to remove it.

Fix: Delete the branch at :452-472 outright. The general path beneath it produces the correct row for every shape the branch handles, plus the correct row for the four shapes it gets wrong, and the full suite passes without it. If it is kept instead, route it through `promotedRowsAccountForParent` rather than returning the parent unconditionally — but deletion is smaller, safer, and is what the evidence supports.

Evidence: Probe through the real `makeAsNonChildTransactions` (temporary file, deleted after; sweep run against both this branch and `main`). Parent 12345 with ONE child of 20000, child unsplit -> `updated [{id:'p', amount:12345, is_parent:false, error:null}]`, `deleted [{id:'c0', amount:20000}]` — the user's typed 200.00 is destroyed and the row reads 123.45. Byte-identical output on `main` (`1-child, parent 12345, child 20000: upd p:12345 | del c0:20000` on both versions), so this is untouched pre-existing behaviour, not a regression. The two-child equivalent is covered and correct: parent 12345 with children 7000/7000 -> `updated [[c0:7000],[c1:7000]]`, parent deleted, surplus preserved. Reachability is narrow and I could not construct it: the register's Split affordance (`makeEmptySplitSubtransactions`, :84-90) always creates TWO children, so `childTransactions.length === 1` needs a split already reduced to one leg. The work order records the same gap as unknowns[2]. That narrowness is why this is minor rather than major — it is a real hole under the invariant the new comment at :484-490 states as general ('A shortfall says the same thing'), but no known UI gesture reaches it and the PR does not make it worse.

Fix: Either bring the early return under the same relation (promote the child when it accounts for the parent, keep the parent when it does not), or add a line to its comment saying the branch deliberately keeps the parent's own amount and why. As shipped it is a comment asserting a shared invariant above a branch that does not implement it — the same defect shape as the stale header comment this PR removed from the test file.
